transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-17
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Priya (ZenWave Platform), Marco (ZenWave SRE), Eli (ZenWave ML)
Links shared: runbook (https://redwood.internal/trace-runbook), sample dashboard (https://dash.redwood/zenwave-sample)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive focused on mapping Redwood runtime spans to token-level metrics, correlating KV cache hits/misses with per-token latency, and how to wire OTLP traces into ZenWave's Splunk/OTel collector. Agreed to run bench with dedicated pool and share sample traces + config.

Topics covered:
- Per-token span design (attributes: token_index, model_variant, kv_hit, batch_size, sequence_pos)
- OTLP exporter config and sampling decisions (head-based vs tail-based vs probabilistic)
- KV cache heatmap + correlation with latency spikes
- Batching behavior and how continuous batching shows up in traces
- Quantization impact on token latency variance (int8 vs fp16)
- VPC/on-prem considerations for OTLP endpoints and egress constraints

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for carving out time, this is Maya from Redwood, i'm joined by Liam our runtime se. how are you all doing?
[00:12] Priya: doing great, thanks. we wanted to go deeper on token level tracing — our SREs keep seeing these spikes and we can't map them to anything obvious.
[00:20] Marco: yeah we see periodic 200–400ms blips that correlate with production traffic bursts, not sure if it's kv cache churn or batching.
[00:30] Liam: okay, good. quick note, the way Redwood emits spans today is per-request with optional per-token child spans — we usually call them token_span or token_emit, and we include attributes like token_index, model_variant, kv_hit boolean, and batch_size. sometimes the exporter mangles the names, you'll see tokenIdx or token-index depending on OTLP mapping.
[01:05] Eli: are these token spans on by default? is there large overhead?
[01:12] Liam: by default we emit minimal per-token metrics: token_count and a summarized timing. per-token spans are off by default for hosted because of volume, but you can enable them per-route or per-customer with sampling rules. overhead is proportional to tokens emitted — we've seen ~5–12% CPU increase on the host when you enable full per-token spans at high qps, but you can mitigate with tail-sampling and attribute filtering.
[02:00] Marco: ok, we're on a private deployment (VPC) so we can tweak. our exporter sits behind a collector in the VPC — any gotchas there?
[02:12] Liam: yeah, two main gotchas: 1) egress/MTU and batching — OTLP over gRPC chunks a lot of spans and you need to tune collector receive_batch_size, 2) TLS and KMS for keying the export stream if you're routing across regions. Also make sure your collector's memory limits can handle token-span bursts.
[03:05] Priya: can you show an example span payload for a token span? trying to map it to our schema.
[03:12] Maya: sure i'll paste a short snippet after the call but here's an annotated example — span.name = "rw.token", attributes: {"token_index": 12, "kv_hit": true, "model_variant": "redwood-medium-q4_0", "batch_id": "b-1234", "seq_len": 128, "gpu_ms": 2.4}. then parent span is the request span with route id and customer id.
[04:00] Eli: that kv_hit flag — how reliable is it? like race conditions where cache warms mid-request?
[04:10] Liam: good question. kv_hit is set at the time of the token generation attempt against the local KV layer. If a remote fetch returns with low latency it shows as hit in downstream but you can see intermediate spikes. We recommend emitting both kv_probe_time and kv_hit so you can separate fast remote hits vs local hits.
[05:20] Marco: we also want to link GPU metrics to tokens — can we attach GPU counters per-token?
[05:28] Liam: you can attach coarse GPU counters: token_gpu_ms or gpu_util_snapshot. High-frequency GPU counters per-token are noisy — we usually emit aggregate per-batch GPU time and then attribute to tokens with batch_size so you can compute average. If you need exact attribution we can add a sampled per-token gpu_ms but expect overhead.
[06:30] Priya: about sampling — what do you recommend? we don't want to lose tail latency insights.
[06:38] Liam: we typically suggest a hybrid: head-based sampling for voluminous baseline (e.g., 1% of requests full token spans) plus deterministic sampling for errors or high-latency requests (capture anything > X ms). Also use attribute-based tail sampling in OTel collector to keep traces with kv_miss=true or latency>200ms.
[07:20] Eli: ok, say we configure head 0.5% plus capture errors — how will that show up in our dashboards?
[07:28] Maya: you'll see general distributions from the sampled traces and full histograms from our aggregated token metrics (which are lower cardinality counters we can also emit). Spans are for deep root-cause. We recommend storing token histograms (per-route, per-model-variant) in your metrics backend and use traces to investigate anomalies.
[08:15] Marco: question on continuous batching — we see variable batch sizes, 1 up to 16 — does Redwood emit batch_size attr?
[08:22] Liam: yes, batch_size is emitted, and you can also get batch_latency and the per-batch token_count. One tricky thing is inter-request batching where multiple requests share the KV cache snapshot; we emit a batch_id so you can correlate multiple request spans to the same batch.
[09:10] Priya: any examples of dashboards you've seen that correlate KV hit heatmap with latency?
[09:18] Maya: yes we have a sample dashboard — heatmap x-axis = time, y-axis = kv_hit_rate (binned by prefix), color = p95 token latency. There's also a matrix that groups by model_variant and quantization profile. link: https://dash.redwood/zenwave-sample
[09:52] Eli: about quantization — we've tried int8 quant on our internal models and saw lower median but more variance on long sequences. does Redwood's runtime behave similarly?
[10:02] Liam: absolutely. lower precision reduces per-token time significantly for short sequences, but for long sequences the kv cache and memory bandwidth can dominate and you may see variance. We emit quant_profile attr (e.g., q4_0, int8, fp16) so you can bucket latencies by profile. Important: quantized kernels sometimes have different warmup characteristics — you'll see cold-cache spikes.
[11:05] Marco: can we tag traces with deployment zone? we need to debug region fallback behavior.
[11:12] Liam: yes deployment_zone, region, and node_id are emitted on the request span. For private deployments you can also configure node labels to match your k8s/node naming.
[12:00] Priya: Our biggest blocker is mapping spikes to KV churn — what would you recommend as a correlation strategy?
[12:10] Liam: two-pronged: 1) create a rolling join between token_latency_histogram and kv_hit_rate per-prefix (5s buckets). 2) Annotate traces where kv_probe_time>threshold and link to batch_id. Practically that's a dashboard with two panes: a heatmap of kv_hit_rate and an overlaid p95 token latency.
[13:08] Eli: is there any off-by-one or ordering problem with token_index in traces when batching?
[13:15] Liam: yes if multiple requests are interleaved in the same batch the token_index is relative to the request, but we also emit global_batch_position which is the index inside the batch stream — that helps reassembly. You'll see weird ordering if your collector rearranges spans but we've seen that mostly with naive span exporters that buffer per-thread.
[14:20] Marco: what about trace size — if we enable per-token spans we risk collector OOMs, right?
[14:28] Liam: yep, collector memory is the usual choke point. To avoid OOMs: increase receive batch size, use grpc compression, enable tail-sampling to drop non-interesting traces, or use sidecar-based local buffering with firewall egress rules.
[15:05] Priya: hypothetically, can we push token metrics as OTLP metrics rather than spans to reduce cardinality?
[15:12] Liam: yes that's a pattern we recommend — emit per-token aggregates as OTLP metrics (counters/histograms) keyed by low-cardinality attributes (route, model_variant, seq_len_bucket, kv_hit boolean). Spans remain for detailed investigation.
[16:00] Eli: do you have any canonical attribute naming? our infra enforces snake_case.
[16:08] Maya: we can provide a canonical mapping. Redwood uses snake_case by default for OTLP but some older SDKs used camelCase; we'll send you the canonical table in the runbook link.
[16:45] Marco: VPC specifics — our security team requires local-only egress and will not allow Redwood's hosted collectors to pull telemetry. can we run collector on-prem and still use Redwood console dashboards?
[16:55] Liam: yes, you can run a collector in your VPC that forwards aggregated metrics only to Redwood's control plane over a secure channel. For traces we recommend sending sampled spans (only the sampled ones) if you want deep links from Redwood Console. Otherwise you can host everything and point Redwood to metrics endpoints via a read-only pull with mTLS. There are options.
[18:00] Priya: will RBAC or PII filters be applied to spans? we have sensitive prompt tokens.
[18:10] Maya: yes, Redwood supports attribute scrubbing at the runtime layer — you can drop prompt text or replace it with a hash before spans are emitted. We also recommend token-level redaction: never emit full token text; use token_id and token_hash instead.
[19:05] Eli: oh that explains some of our earlier logs — we saw full token text in older traces. okay we'll scrub.
[19:20] Marco: how do we verify that kv_miss events correlate with remote fetch cost?
[19:28] Liam: emit kv_probe_time_ms attribute and also include kv_source (local|remote|disk). then do a scatter plot of kv_probe_time_ms vs token_latency and color by kv_source. That will show correlation.
[20:10] Priya: any recommended thresholds for kv_probe_time to trigger alerts?
[20:18] Liam: for SSD-backed remote fetches maybe >5ms; for network calls >20ms. But this depends on your SLOs. We usually set alert if kv_miss_rate bumps 2x baseline and p95 token latency increases >30ms.
[21:02] Eli: can Redwood inject an idempotency key across batch boundaries to help correlate request retries?
[21:10] Liam: yes request_id and idempotency_key exist and are emitted on request span; they survive retries.
[22:00] Marco: we want to see a demo of our traces in your sample dashboard with our traces. can you walk through what you'd need?
[22:08] Maya: we need 3 sample trace files in OTLP/JSON or zip of the collector traces, and a mapping file for your attribute names — send to maya@redwood.com. We'll ingest and create a private dashboard.
[23:15] Priya: ok we'll prepare that. For the bench: what config should we use to reproduce the spikes? kv hit/miss patterns?
[23:25] Liam: simulate a cold-start workload with 20% novel prefixes (forced kv_miss), mixed sequence lengths (16/128/512), and burst qps to expose batching behavior. We'll provide the bench script.
[24:10] Eli: curious: we've heard of token-span aggregation as an alternative to per-token spans — what is that?
[24:18] Liam: token-span aggregation collapses many token spans into a compressed structure emitted as a single span with an embedded histogram or proto-blob. It reduces span count but preserves granularity. Downside: harder to query in some tracing backends.
[25:05] Marco: what about exporters — OTLP over http vs grpc for high throughput?
[25:12] Liam: grpc is higher throughput and lower CPU in our tests; http can be simpler to open to collectors. Use grpc with compression for heavy token-span workloads.
[26:00] Priya: any gotchas on sequence length buckets? we have variable lengths so p95 gets skewed.
[26:08] Liam: bucket by seq_len ranges (1-64,65-256,257-1024) and compute per-bucket p50/p95. Redwood emits seq_len attr so you can build those buckets in your metrics backend.
[27:00] Eli: I'd like to understand how quantization/not quantization shows up in perf traces — do you have examples?
[27:08] Liam: yes we have before/after traces that show throughput jump but tail spikes on large sequences due to memory copy overhead. We'll attach in the runbook examples.
[28:15] Marco: what about tracing across model variants when fallback happens? i.e., switch from redwood-large to redwood-medium for cost fallback.
[28:24] Liam: we set model_variant on spans and emit a fallback_reason attr. You can then filter for traces where fallback_reason != null and measure end-user latency delta.
[29:00] Priya: how long will the sample dashboard retention be?
[29:05] Maya: by default 30 days for demo dashboards, we can extend for enterprise customers.
[29:50] Eli: okay one sec — small noise — when you said token_hash vs token_text, can you confirm token_hash is reversible?
[29:58] Liam: no token_hash should be one-way (sha256). don't store any mapping unless you have a strict use-case and governance.
[31:00] Marco: can Redwood help with collector autoscaling recommendations? our collector pods were crashing previously when we enabled more spans.
[31:08] Liam: yes, increase collector replicas, tune recv_batch_size, and enable ingress rate limiting. We also have a lightweight sidecar that batches and back-pressures the local process. We'll share sizing guidance based on your qps.
[32:10] Priya: let's talk about the bench next steps — we want to include 3 scenarios: cold kv miss heavy, steady-state high-qps with batching, and mixed quant profiles.
[32:22] Liam: that's perfect. For cold kv: set prefix churn to 50% and throttle background refresh. For steady-state: 1–2% novel requests, target qps 400. For mixed quant: run int8 vs fp16 vs q4_0 combinations across 50% traffic.
[33:10] Eli: will Redwood provide a script to capture the OTLP export from the collector into a file we can share?
[33:18] Maya: yes we'll provide a short collector config snippet and a script that uses otelcol to dump traces to file.
[34:05] Marco: security question — how do we authenticate exporter traffic from private collector to Redwood?
[34:12] Liam: mutual TLS + token-based short-lived certs via your KMS is common. We also support static mTLS and dedicated peering. We'll document options.
[35:00] Priya: what about cost — increasing exported spans will increase egress and storage costs, any ballpark?
[35:08] Maya: depends on sampling. A rough rule: full token spans at steady qps can increase telemetry volume 10–30x. With 0.5–1% sampling and targeted tail capture you can keep it within 2–3x. We'll help estimate using your qps numbers.
[36:20] Eli: are there Redwood Console integrations for Splunk/Datadog?
[36:28] Maya: yes we have connectors that pull sampled spans and metrics into Datadog and Splunk; for private deployments we provide an inbound webhook with mTLS.
[37:10] Marco: can we get the mapping of Redwood internal metric names to OTel/Prometheus names? our ops team wants to automate alerts.
[37:18] Liam: yes we'll include a mapping table in the runbook.
[38:00] Priya: any recommended SLOs for token latency?
[38:08] Liam: many customers use per-token p95 < 80ms for chat-like flows, and end-to-end request p95 < 300ms depending on sequence length. But your SLOs may vary.
[39:05] Eli: minor: we've seen weird collector timestamps leading to negative spans when clocks drift. suggestions?
[39:12] Liam: enable NTP across nodes and the collector; use monotonic timestamps if your tracer supports it — we also include span.sync_time to help.
[40:00] Marco: if we do the bench and find kv misses are the main culprit, options are: increase cache size, prefetch common prefixes, or pin dedicated warm pool. is Redwood able to allocate dedicated warm pools?
[40:10] Liam: yes, on Dedicated we can reserve pinned GPU pools and pre-warm KV with a preload job. For Private, we'll provide the preload tooling.
[41:05] Priya: let's talk about alerts — we want automatic trace capture when p95 jumps.
[41:12] Liam: you'd set a metric alert on p95 token latency; the alert triggers collector to increase sampling or mark the next N traces for full capture. That's doable with an alert webhook to your collector.
[42:00] Eli: ok, we're comfortable. two asks: we want the config snippet and a small POC where Redwood ingests our 3 traces into the sample dashboard.
[42:08] Maya: got it. we'll send config + sample dashboard after the call.
[43:00] Marco: also want to schedule the bench — week of the 29th works.
[43:05] Maya: i'll follow up with a calendar invite — Liam will run the bench.
[43:40] Priya: one last question — what metrics should we keep long-term vs short-term?
[43:48] Liam: keep token histogram summaries and kv_hit_rate long-term (90 days+), trace payloads short term (30 days) unless you need compliance. token spans are heavyweight to retain.
[45:00] Eli: cool. quick nit: sometimes the token_index and batch_position both show up — which is canonical?
[45:08] Liam: token_index is canonical per-request, batch_position is for reassembly across the batch. Use both if you want to reconstitute.
[46:00] Maya: recap — action items: Maya send runbook + OTLP snippet, Liam prepares bench script, Priya uploads sample traces. We schedule bench week of 2026-09-29.
[46:18] Priya: sounds good. thanks all.
[47:00] Marco: thanks — appreciate the level of detail.
[47:05] Eli: thanks everyone.
[57:50] Maya: bye all, we'll follow up in email with artifacts.

End of transcript.
